name: Blepharoplasty
lead: Blepharoplasty, commonly called eyelid surgery, is plastic surgery that removes or repositions excess skin, muscle and fat of the upper or lower eyelids and can extend to reinforcing the surrounding muscle and tendon support. It is done for functional reasons, such as heavy upper lids that reduce peripheral vision, and for cosmetic reasons, such as reducing hooding, smoothing the lid-cheek transition or reducing under-eye bags.[8][1][4][26]

The appearance payoff is the eye area: the upper lid is opened up and shows more of the eye and lash line, the lower lid is smoothed, and a tired or puffy look can be reduced. The American Society of Plastic Surgeons lists loose upper-lid skin that folds or changes the lid's shape, fat deposits that cause puffiness, bags beneath the eyes, drooping lower lids that expose white below the iris, and excess lower-lid skin with fine wrinkles among the things the operation can address.[26] In East Asian practice a distinct variant, double-eyelid surgery, creates or raises an upper-lid crease and is among the most common cosmetic operations in several countries.[24][8]

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a hardmaxxing option for the eye area, often alongside fat grafting, brow repositioning or canthal procedures, and members debate whether it would improve eye shape, ptosis, or perceived tiredness.[21][22][23]

Reviews describe upper blepharoplasty as having both aesthetic and functional outcomes, and a 2023 systematic review compared techniques and outcomes including effects on the cornea, intraocular pressure, dry eye and visual quality.[1] A 2026 review characterised modern practice as having shifted from subtractive techniques toward tissue preservation and augmentation.[5] Wikipedia notes the procedure is more common in women (about 85% of US cases in 2014 and 88% in the UK).[8]

paras: The word comes from Greek roots meaning eyelid and moulded or formed. Surgeons work on the zone from the brow to the upper cheek, removing or repositioning skin and fat, tightening supporting tissue and, in lower-lid work, re-draping fat to smooth the transition from lid to cheek.[8]

Upper blepharoplasty uses an incision in the natural eyelid crease to remove or reposition skin, muscle and sometimes fat; it can be cosmetic or functional. Lower blepharoplasty can be transcutaneous (incision just beneath the lashes, used when there is significant skin laxity) or transconjunctival (inside the lid, leaving no external scar but suited to patients with little excess skin, who may need a separate procedure for skin tightening).[8][4]

Contemporary lower blepharoplasty increasingly includes relocating orbital fat to correct inferior orbital hollowing, tear trough deformity and lid-cheek junction effacement rather than only removing fat.[4] An influential 1995 paper on arcus marginalis release and orbital fat preservation argued that conventional fat removal can create a concave contour deformity in the lower lids.[12]

Adjunctive techniques include canthopexy or canthoplasty to stabilise the outer corner of the lid, fat repositioning along the infraorbital rim for tear trough deformities, and autologous fat transfer to restore periorbital volume.[8] Newer variants include pinch blepharoplasty for the lower lid[14] and office-based approaches.[15] A CO2 laser can replace the scalpel; Wikipedia lists less bleeding, shorter surgery and less bruising among the benefits claimed for it and notes a debate over whether laser work counts as surgery.[8]

The eyelid is built in layers: skin, subcutaneous tissue, the orbicularis oculi muscle, the orbital septum, orbital fat, the tarsal plate and the conjunctiva. The upper lid has medial and central fat compartments and is lifted by the levator palpebrae superioris; the lower lid has medial, central and lateral compartments and meets the cheek at the tear trough.[8]

With age the skin loosens, the septum weakens, fat herniates forward and volume is lost, producing upper-lid hooding and lower-lid contour irregularities.[8] Excess lid skin is called dermatochalasis. It most often affects older adults, can begin from about age 40, affects men and women equally and can be acquired or congenital; in severe cases it can block part of the upper visual field.[25] Blepharoplasty is the usual treatment, and upper-lid surgery performed only for appearance, along with most lower-lid surgery, is generally regarded as cosmetic.[25]

Excess upper-lid skin can drape over the lashes and reduce the visual field, making driving and reading harder; lower-lid indications include excess skin, weakened septum, fat bulging and malposition.[8][25]

People seek surgery to reduce under-eye bags or upper-lid hooding associated with ageing, and to restore a smoother lid-cheek line.[8][26] A systematic review of treatments for periorbital hyperpigmentation (dark circles) concluded that fillers and fat grafting were most effective where volume loss is the cause, and that blepharoplasty was best where excess skin laxity is the underlying cause, while noting limited high-quality evidence.[27]
East Asian double-eyelid surgery creates or raises a supratarsal fold; one study describes a three-mini-incision technique for this purpose.[7][8]

This variant creates an upper-lid crease in people who lack one, with the aim of making the eyes look larger and more expressive. Wikipedia reports that natural crease rates vary by study, from about 41 percent of Koreans to 70 to 83 percent of Chinese and Japanese women, so the operation is not only about adding a feature people never have.[24]

Wikipedia credits Dr Kotaro Mikamo with performing the first such operation in Japan in 1896. Historians disagree about his motive: one view is that he aimed to make Japanese eyes look more Western, while another cites Mikamo's own description of the single lid as monotonous and expressionless as evidence that he aimed to enhance existing Japanese aesthetics.[24]

Unlike Western upper blepharoplasty, where removing excess skin is often enough, the fold must be anchored by sutures that attach to the septoaponeurotic junction.[24] Non-incisional (suture-ligation) methods are quicker with shorter recovery, but the crease is described as less durable; incisional methods give a more lasting, dynamic crease and can remove excess skin and fat but take longer to heal, with lagophthalmos (incomplete eyelid closure) a major risk.[24] Epicanthoplasty is often performed alongside.[24] Wikipedia reports it as the most common aesthetic procedure in Taiwan and South Korea[24] and notes that in South Korea it costs roughly US$2,000 to $4,000, with many foreigners travelling there for it.[8] Several of these technique statements are flagged as needing citations on Wikipedia.

The 2023 systematic review of upper blepharoplasty included 20 studies and nine in the meta-analysis, covering six surgery types and outcomes such as intraocular pressure, central corneal thickness, keratometry, corneal astigmatism, visual acuity, Schirmer tests, tear film break-up time and the Ocular Surface Disease Index. Its meta-analysis found no significant differences between techniques on these measures.[1]

A registered study is evaluating patient-reported outcomes with the FACE-Q instrument in 90 patients with upper-lid dermatochalasis,[17] and others are assessing functional changes and vision quality after upper blepharoplasty.[18][19] Registered trials also compare skin-only with skin-plus-orbicularis resection with respect to dry eye and meibomian gland outcomes[30] and a small-incision technique against standard upper blepharoplasty for medial fat removal.[29]
Wikipedia describes typical results as smoother lid contours and a more defined lid-cheek junction, varying with anatomy and technique.[8]

Swelling and bruising are common and usually resolve in weeks.[8] A randomised trial examined compression dressings after upper blepharoplasty for edema, ecchymosis, pain and ocular surface irritation.[11] Reviews describe dry eye and effects on ocular surface and cornea as outcomes assessed after upper blepharoplasty,[1] and lower lid malposition, scleral show and ectropion as complications of lower-lid surgery that canthal support aims to reduce.[4][8]

In 1987 a cluster of Mycobacterium chelonae wound infections after plastic surgery was traced to a contaminated gentian violet skin-marking solution.[13] Wikipedia's article is itself flagged as needing more reliable medical references and has no dedicated complications section.[8]

Dermatochalasis has been the target of energy-based skin tightening. A clinical study of microplasma described it as a non-surgical option and noted that surgical blepharoplasty remains the gold standard,[16] and a separate trial evaluated plasma exeresis as a non-surgical technique.[28] For brow position, a randomised trial compared two techniques of surgical eyebrow suspension.[31]

Greek and Roman physicians recorded eyelid techniques; Aulus Cornelius Celsus described cutting the skin to relax the lids in De Medicina in the first century. Karl Ferdinand von Graefe coined the term blepharoplasty in 1818 while describing repairs of eyelid deformities after cancer.[8] Double-eyelid surgery emerged in Japan in 1896 under Mikamo.[24] Later developments include the shift to fat preservation and midface integration described in the 1990s literature[12] and the broader move toward tissue preservation and augmentation described in 2026.[5]

Human evidence includes a systematic review and meta-analysis of upper blepharoplasty,[1] a systematic review of treatments for periorbital hyperpigmentation that places blepharoplasty within the options,[27] randomised trials of compression dressings after upper blepharoplasty[11] and of eyebrow suspension techniques,[31] case series of mini-incision double-eyelid technique,[7] and non-surgical alternatives such as microplasma for dermatochalasis, a clinical trial.[16] Registered studies address FACE-Q outcomes, functional changes, vision quality and fat preservation.[17][18][19][20]

On looksmax.org, members ask whether upper and lower blepharoplasty with fat grafts would 'ascend' the eye area, and some repliers suggest brow repositioning as an alternative.[21] Others discuss whether surgery would resolve ptosis-related asymmetry when the eyeballs or orbits themselves appear asymmetric.[22] Members also list blepharoplasty among multiple procedures in before-and-after posts alongside jaw surgery, rhinoplasty, hair transplant and fat transfer.[23]

Eye-area plans in these threads often bundle several operations; surgical literature likewise treats lid, brow, fat and midface as interacting structures, which is why adjunct procedures appear in both settings.[4][8]

lore.intro: Blepharoplasty is discussed on looksmax.org as a way to change eyelid appearance and as one element of multi-procedure eye-area plans, often with fat grafting or brow work.[21][22][23]

claims.claim: Blepharoplasty with fat grafting can 'ascend' the eye area.
claims.believers: A poster plans upper and lower blepharoplasty with lower-lid fat grafts and later supra-brow grafts, while a replier suggests brow repositioning instead.[21]
claims.experts: Reviews describe lower blepharoplasty with fat relocation for hollowing and note surgeons' use of fat preservation; outcomes research on the combined aim was not located.[4][12]

claims.claim: Eyelid surgery can fix a droopy or ptotic eye and its apparent asymmetry.
claims.believers: One poster hoped blepharoplasty would correct a ptosis eye but doubts it would if the eyes or orbits are themselves asymmetric.[22]
claims.experts: Blepharoplasty addresses excess skin, muscle and fat; Wikipedia describes the operation as correcting excess skin, muscle and fat, and brow position and ptosis are treated by other procedures; no trial located addresses whether blepharoplasty alone corrects ptosis-related asymmetry.[8]

claims.claim: Blepharoplasty reliably removes tired-looking bags and hooding.
claims.believers: Members cite wanting to remove lines and bags and report plans for surgery.[21]
claims.experts: Surgical reviews describe it as the established treatment for dermatochalasis and bags, with non-surgical options such as microplasma under study.[8][16]

claims.claim: Double-eyelid surgery is a way to westernise the eyes.
claims.believers: Some historians and commentators read the operation's origins in Meiji-era Japan as an attempt to make eyes look more Western.[24]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes the view is contested: natural double eyelids are common in East Asian populations, and Mikamo's own words are cited as favouring an aim of enhancing existing Japanese aesthetics.[24]

claims.claim: Fat preservation gives a more youthful result than fat removal.
claims.believers: Members planning fat grafts to the lower lid or supra-brow area describe volume as part of the goal.[21]
claims.experts: Surgical papers from 1995 onward argue that removing lower-lid fat can create hollowing, and a 2026 review describes the field's move toward preservation and augmentation.[12][5]

claims.claim: Blepharoplasty can address dark under-eye circles.
claims.believers: Eye-area plans on forums list it among options for tired-looking eyes.[21]
claims.experts: A systematic review found blepharoplasty best suited to dark circles caused by excess skin laxity, with fillers and fat grafting favoured where volume loss is the cause, and noted limited high-quality evidence.[27]

card.summary: Eyelid surgery to remove or reposition excess skin and fat; established for hooding and bags, with no trials for looksmaxxing-specific eye-shape goals.
card.note: Dry eye and lower-lid malposition are documented risks; fat preservation is increasingly emphasised.

quick.overview:
Blepharoplasty is the standard operation for droopy upper lids and lower-lid bags, removing or repositioning skin, muscle and fat. Surgeons also perform it to improve vision when lids obstruct sight, and East Asian double-eyelid surgery is one of the most common variants.

Looksmaxxing members discuss it for eye shape, ptosis and tiredness, usually combined with fat grafts or brow work. Surgical literature supports it for dermatochalasis and bags; claims about dramatic eye-shape changes are mainly forum accounts.
quick.mechanism: Incisions in the lid crease (upper) or beneath the lashes or inside the lid (lower) allow removal, repositioning or preservation of skin, muscle and fat. Canthal support may be added to stabilise the lower lid.
quick.risks: Swelling and bruising are common for weeks; dry eye, lid malposition and asymmetry are reported complications, and a 1987 infection cluster was traced to contaminated skin-marking solution. Surgeons often combine it with canthal support to reduce malposition.
